samples.moment: On 28 April 1967, at the induction centre in Houston, his name was called and he did not step forward. Within hours the boxing authorities moved to strip his title. He did not fight again for three and a half years, and he did not change his account of why.
samples.why: Chosen because there are weeks when you have to say where you stand, out loud, and keep saying it.
samples.source: Not yet sourced. Several versions of his best-known line on the war circulate; none is confirmed.
samples.gist: He did not step forward, and did not change his account of why.

samples.moment: She had turned Bobby Riggs down. Then Margaret Court accepted, and lost. King understood what a second loss would cost every woman in the game, and said yes. On 20 September 1973, in the Houston Astrodome, in front of more than thirty thousand people and a vast television audience, she won in straight sets.
samples.pattern: I thought it would set us back 50 years if I didn't win that match.
samples.why: Chosen because the thing you've been avoiding gets more expensive every week you wait.
samples.source: billiejeanking.com, “Battle of the Sexes”; check quote against a primary interview.
samples.gist: She took the match she had turned down, once waiting cost more.
samples.walk: take the conversation you've been avoiding, and set its terms.
move_examples: This week, put the conversation you have been avoiding in the diary, and open it by naming what the two of you will decide. Ten minutes.
At the team meeting, say yes to the thing you turned down, and say why waiting costs more. One minute.
line_examples: To the colleague you have been putting off: Let's settle it this week. Here is when, and here is what we decide.
To your team: I said no once. I'm saying yes now, because waiting costs all of us more.

samples.moment: Branch Rickey wanted him to break baseball's colour line, and spent the meeting acting out the abuse he would face — the slurs, the spikes, the umpires. Robinson asked if Rickey wanted a player who was afraid to fight back. Rickey said no. He agreed to take it, without answering, for his first seasons.
samples.pattern: I'm looking for a ballplayer with guts enough not to fight back.
samples.why: Chosen because, for a while, your restraint will say more than anything you could answer back.
samples.source: Robinson, I Never Had It Made (1972). Check wording.
samples.caution: The restraint was a condition of the deal. Robinson spoke out forcefully once it lifted.
samples.gist: He agreed to take it without answering, for a while.
samples.walk: let the first reaction pass without an answer.

samples.moment: Opening night of the 2016 Democratic convention, in the ugliest campaign in memory. She never named the opponent. She talked about raising two daughters in the White House, and about what she and her husband told them to do when someone was cruel.
samples.pattern: When they go low, we go high.
samples.why: Chosen because the room will be watching how you respond, more than what you say.
samples.walk: don't name the person. Say what you stand for, and let the room compare.
move_examples: At the team meeting after a cruel remark, leave its author unnamed; say what the team stands for, then move to the next item. One minute.
line_examples: To your team, after a cruel remark in the meeting: We won't answer that in kind. Here is what we stand for, and we'll hold to it.
To a peer who wants you to hit back: Let the room compare us. I won't attack; watch what we do next.

samples.moment: Weeks earlier he had beaten Hillary Clinton in a primary that ran seventeen months. Four weeks after the election he named her Secretary of State — the senior post in his cabinet — and announced it standing next to her, with the rest of his national security team.
samples.why: Chosen because, like you, he had to lead alongside someone who had wanted his job.
samples.source: NPR, “Obama Unveils National Security Team,” 1 Dec 2008.
samples.gist: He gave his rival the senior post, and stood next to her to announce it.
samples.walk: give the person who wanted your job the senior seat, and stand next to them when you say it.
move_examples: At the first team meeting, give the colleague who wanted the job the senior seat on the biggest piece of work, and announce it standing beside them. Two minutes.
line_examples: To the colleague who wanted the job: I want you in the senior seat on this, and I'll say so in front of the team.
To your team: They were the strongest candidate for this job, and that is why they lead this work. I'm standing beside them as I say it.

samples.moment: Video of his former pastor's sermons was running on every channel. He did not issue a short statement and move on. On 18 March 2008, at the National Constitution Center in Philadelphia, he gave a long speech on race in America — condemning the remarks, refusing to disown the man, and naming the grievance on more than one side.
samples.pattern: I can no more disown him than I can disown the black community.
samples.why: Chosen because this week everything you say will be read for what it means as well as what it says.
samples.source: “A More Perfect Union,” transcript, National Constitution Center.
samples.gist: He said the hardest part himself, at length, once.
samples.walk: say the hardest part yourself, before anyone else frames it.
move_examples: At the team meeting, say the hardest part of the news yourself, in your own words, before anyone else can frame it. Three minutes.
line_examples: To your team, before the rumour reaches them: Here is the hard part, in my words, before anyone else tells it.
To your boss: I'm going to address it in full this week, in my own words. Here is the outline.

samples.moment: He turned twenty-one in May 1971 and his Motown contract ended. He did not re-sign on the old terms. He recorded on his own, then went back to the label with the work in hand. The contract he signed gave him control of his own records.
samples.why: Chosen because the work is yours, and so is how it reaches people.
samples.source: Music of My Mind release history; check against a primary biography.
samples.caution: Royalty figures that circulate online are unverified. Do not add them.
samples.gist: He went back to the label with the finished work in hand.
samples.walk: put your name on the work. You built it.
move_examples: In your next client meeting, bring the finished piece and present it yourself, with your name on the cover. Twenty minutes.
line_examples: To your manager: This work is mine. I want my name on it when it goes out.
To the client lead: I'll bring the finished piece to the meeting, and I'll present it myself.

samples.moment: Langley, Virginia, late 1950s: Johnson, a mathematician in the Flight Research Division, did calculations the engineers built on, yet the engineers' briefings where the space work was decided were closed to the women computers. She kept asking to attend and asked whether any rule barred her. None did, and she began sitting in. Within a few years flight crews relied on her numbers.
samples.pattern: Is there a law against it?
samples.why: Chosen because getting into the room where it's decided is your work this year.
samples.source: Corpus draft. NASA oral-history interviews describe her asking to attend the briefings; verify the wording.
samples.gist: She asked whether any rule barred her. None did.
samples.walk: ask whether any rule bars you from the room. Then sit in.

samples.moment: Elected president of the Harvard Law Review in February 1990 by a board split into factions, he gave senior posts to editors who had opposed him, including conservatives who had voted against him. Some of his own supporters felt passed over. The Review came out on time.
samples.why: Chosen because the people who didn't back you still have to work with you on Monday.
samples.source: Corpus draft. Remnick, The Bridge (2010); verify the appointments detail.
samples.gist: He gave posts to the editors who had opposed him.
samples.walk: ask the person who ran against you for the number, out loud, in front of the group.

samples.moment: He had run marketing for the founders and left when they would not back his idea. Two years later, in August 1987, he bought the company from them. The first thing he did was make his case in person, in the roasting plant, to people who had known him as a colleague.
samples.why: Chosen because, like you, he had to lead people who remembered him as a peer.
samples.source: Corpus draft. Verify against Schultz, Pour Your Heart Into It (1997).
samples.gist: He made his case in person to people who had known him as a colleague.
samples.walk: let their call stand when you'd have changed it.

samples.moment: On 25 February 1964 he took the heavyweight title from Sonny Liston as Cassius Clay. The next morning he confirmed he was a member of the Nation of Islam, and within weeks he was introducing himself by a new name and insisting on it, whatever the press printed.
samples.pattern: I don't have to be what you want me to be.
samples.why: Chosen because standing on your own name is the work this year.
samples.source: Corpus draft. Press conference, Miami Beach, 26 February 1964; the name followed on 6 March. Verify wording.
samples.gist: Within weeks he was introducing himself by a new name.
samples.walk: say your one thing in the first two minutes, before the credentials.

samples.moment: The Wailers had recorded for other people's labels and seen little of the money. By the end of the decade they had started their own imprint and were putting their records out themselves, selling them from a shop in Trench Town.
samples.why: Chosen because the name on the record is the thing you own.
samples.source: Corpus draft. Verify against White, Catch a Fire (1983).
samples.gist: They put their records out under their own imprint.
samples.walk: leave the credentials slide out, once.

samples.moment: A week before Wimbledon, in a room at the Gloucester Hotel, she got more than sixty women players to agree to form their own association, with her as its first president. The day before, she had been one of them.
samples.why: Chosen because you had to become the person who speaks for people who were your peers.
samples.source: Corpus draft. WTA founding, Gloucester Hotel, 21 June 1973. Verify the numbers.
samples.gist: The day before, she had been one of them.

situations.chip: Nobody told you what the job asks
situations.line: The job changed and nobody said how.

situations.chip: The boss of people who were your peers
situations.line: The people you sat beside now report to you.

situations.chip: Naming a problem nobody sees
situations.line: You inherited a problem and everyone here thinks things are fine.

situations.chip: Following someone they loved
situations.line: The person before you was loved here, and you are measured against them.

situations.chip: Accountable for work you can’t judge
situations.line: You answer for work you could not do yourself.

situations.chip: Getting credit for your work
situations.line: Your work reaches the client in somebody else’s voice.

situations.chip: Not the style they expected
situations.line: You are quiet in meetings, and you are not going to start shouting.

situations.chip: You were told one thing, then another
situations.line: The ask keeps changing under you.

situations.chip: Hard to place
situations.line: People do not know what to do with you.

situations.chip: Saying it in your own words
situations.line: You have to announce yourself, and every draft sounds like everyone else.

situations.chip: Being heard in a room that decides
situations.line: You know the answer and the room does not follow it.

situations.chip: Selling what you used to make
situations.line: You used to do the work. Now you have to win it.

situations.chip: Standing in your own name
situations.line: Clients come for the firm. You want them to come for you.

situations.chip: The decision gets made before the meeting
situations.line: You need people who do not report to you.

situations.chip: More people than you can see
situations.line: Your team is bigger than the people you see each week.

situations.chip: Growing people without a bench
situations.line: The people you used to grow through have gone.

situations.chip: Stopping work people are proud of
situations.line: Something has to stop, and people built it.

situations.chip: Carrying a decision you didn’t make
situations.line: You have to stand behind a call that was not yours.

situations.chip: Everything you do gets read as a signal
situations.line: Everything you do is read for what it means.

situations.chip: Everyone agrees, and nothing moves
situations.line: The room says yes and nothing changes.

situations.chip: Losing what you were best at
situations.line: The promotion took away the work you were best at.

situations.chip: Good at it, and becalmed
situations.line: It works, you are good at it, and you are bored.
